meta.title: Biggest dinosaur: probably Argentinosaurus | Museum of Ages
meta.description: Biggest dinosaur: probably Argentinosaurus, about 30 to 35 m (98 to 115 ft), roughly 65 to 80 t. Size comparison: seven dinosaurs and a person to scale.
meta.og_image_alt: Seven dinosaurs in a row from the side, two with long necks towering over the rest, and a grey person who looks tiny beside them.

labels.og_answer: Probably Argentinosaurus, about 30 to 35 m (98 to 115 ft)

top.answer: Probably Argentinosaurus, a long-necked titanosaur from Argentina: about 30 to 35 m (98 to 115 ft) long and roughly 65 to 80 tonnes, by models from a few bones. Nobody can be sure. No complete skeleton of any of the largest kinds has ever been found, and its relative Patagotitan comes close. Our Argentinosaurus in the picture is 30.6 m (100 ft) long, as long as 18 people, each 1.70 m, laid end to end.
top.answer_more: Biggest means three things. The heaviest was most likely a titanosaur from Patagonia, Argentinosaurus or Patagotitan. The longest is not settled. The tallest was probably Sauroposeidon, its head about 17 m (56 ft) up, by four neck bones.

scale.what: Our seven beside a person 1.70 m tall, to one scale, each as our model is built. Our Spinosaurus is a young animal of about 10 m, about three quarters as long as a grown one, so here it is shorter than our T. rex. A grown Spinosaurus was longer than every T. rex, and most likely lighter.

blocks.nav: Three answers, and the biggest meat-eater
blocks.h: Three answers, and the biggest meat-eater

paras: Most likely a titanosaur from Patagonia, Argentinosaurus or Patagotitan. Argentinosaurus is the best-supported candidate, roughly 65 to 80 tonnes by several models, all from a few bones. Patagotitan, known from at least six animals, was put at 69 tonnes in 2017 and corrected by its own team to about 57 in 2020. Which of the two was bigger is open: they share too few bones to compare. Dreadnoughtus, once put at 59 tonnes, now comes to about 22 to 30.

Nobody knows. The best-known titanosaurs come to about 30 to 37 m (98 to 121 ft) by their bones and casts. Supersaurus, a long-tailed cousin of Diplodocus, was put at 39 to 42 m (128 to 138 ft) in a conference talk of 2021, not yet in a journal.

Probably Sauroposeidon, from Oklahoma, its head about 17 m (56 ft) up. That rests on four neck bones found in 1994, scaled up on the proportions of Brachiosaurus. The Natural History Museum in London notes it may sit nearer the titanosaurs. Weak, but nothing better is known. The tallest skeleton you can visit is Giraffatitan in Berlin, its skull about 13 m (43 ft) up.
: a grown one was just under 14 m (46 ft) in the model of 2022, scaled up from a young skeleton and a loose adult snout. By weight,

: the heaviest known, called Scotty, comes to about 8.9 tonnes, and a big adult was about 12 m (39 ft) long. Giganotosaurus is often named too, but its remains are fragments and its estimates run from about 6.5 to 14 tonnes.

blocks.intro: For each number: where it came from, and what the field makes of it now.

rows.text: The mounted skeleton in the Museo Carmen Funes in Plaza Huincul, built in the 1990s from the few real bones as a guide. A laser scan of 2013 measured it at 39.7 m. That is a sculpture's length, 5 to 10 m more than any estimate from the bones, and 40 m is that figure rounded. The cast in Atlanta is of the same kind, over 123 feet (about 37.5 m) by its museum.

The 100 came from guesses of the 1990s and an early volume model of 80 to 100. The 83 is the scanned mount of 2013 wrapped in a digital skin, so it belongs to the sculpture. Today's models give roughly 65 to 80 tonnes.

The 37 m is its cast in Chicago, built from at least six animals with the missing bones sculpted, not a figure from the describing paper of 2017. The 69 tonnes came from limb-bone girth in that paper, corrected by the same team to about 57 in 2020. A volume study of 2025 puts it over 60 again.

An Indian find whose bones crumbled before they reached a collection. The 175 to 220 tonnes go back, by later accounts, to internet posts of 2001 that their author withdrew. The only peer-reviewed figure, from 2023, is possibly 110 to 170 tonnes, more probably 110 to 130, and with the bones gone nothing can be checked.

One back vertebra, described and drawn in 1878, then lost. A study of 2006, as later accounts report it, scaled it on Diplodocus to 58 m and about 122 tonnes. In 2018 the same author re-read the drawing as another family of sauropod and brought it down to about 30 to 32 m, renamed Maraapunisaurus. Others call the old figure an extreme overestimate.

By later accounts, a figure of 2005 from a loose snout in Milan, scaled up with a relative's proportions to 16 to 18 m. A skeleton model of 2014 gave over 15 m. The model of 2022, built on the young animal from Morocco and the adult snout, comes out just under 14 m, at about 7.4 tonnes.

The Berlin skeleton, which is Giraffatitan. Its skull sits about 13 m up since the remount of 2007, 11.87 m as first built in 1937: the difference is the neck's pose. No height of the American Brachiosaurus was ever measured, and head heights in print run from 9.4 to 13 m by the neck angle chosen.

rows.term: As tall as a six-storey building
rows.text: A magazine's picture of Sauroposeidon from about 2002, after the estimate of about 17 m. The 17 m itself rests on four neck bones. The line belongs to Sauroposeidon, not to Brachiosaurus or Argentinosaurus.

paras: Nobody has ever put a dinosaur on a scale. Only bones are left, and most of a body is flesh. Every weight here is a sum, made one of three ways.

points: measure around the thigh bone and the upper arm bone, then apply the rule that links girth to weight in animals alive today. The further from anything alive, the shakier it gets. Argentinosaurus has no arm bone at all.
build a body around the skeleton, take its volume, then multiply by a density. The outline is a choice: an adult T. rex comes out anywhere from under 6 to over 18 tonnes.
borrow a better-known cousin, assume its proportions and stretch them to the few bones found. Every length for Argentinosaurus was made this way.

paras: A tape on a museum mount gives an exact number, but for the mount, which is partly sculpture.

Argentinosaurus huinculensis is known from one animal, MCF-PVPH-1, found in the late 1980s about 8 km east of Plaza Huincul in Neuquén, Argentina. What survives: six or seven incomplete back vertebrae, the lower part of the hips, one piece of rib and one calf bone 1.55 m long. No head, neck, tail, shoulder, arm or foot. The bones are kept in the Museo Municipal Carmen Funes in Plaza Huincul. Two huge thigh bones might belong to it, or might not.

Patagotitan mayorum is the best known of the largest kinds. At least six young adults came from a single quarry on a ranch in Chubut, Argentina: the first bone in 2012, more than a hundred bones in all. They are kept at the Museo Paleontológico Egidio Feruglio in Trelew, where a real thigh bone over 2 m long stands beside the cast.

Brachiosaurus altithorax rests on one partial skeleton, FMNH P 25107, dug up in 1900 in western Colorado and kept at the Field Museum in Chicago. Found were seven back vertebrae, the sacrum, two tail vertebrae, a shoulder bone, the right upper arm bone, the right thigh bone, both hip blades and some ribs. No head, neck, forearms, lower legs or feet, and almost no tail, from an animal not yet full grown. About ten finds of the kind are known, none close to complete.

The tall skeleton in Berlin's Museum für Naturkunde is not Brachiosaurus but Giraffatitan brancai, a close African relative. It was dug up at Tendaguru in what is now Tanzania between 1909 and 1913, in the colonial period the museum itself names. The two were split into separate genera in 2009, on at least 26 differences in the bones, and almost every picture of Brachiosaurus shows the African animal. The Berlin mount combines several animals and is, by the museum's own words, the largest mounted dinosaur skeleton in the world.

scale.alt: Our Argentinosaurus as a skeleton from the side: a few dark red back, hip and leg bones among pale restored and borrowed ones, beside the grey person.
scale.key: Dark red: all that was ever found of this animal. Six or seven back vertebrae, the lower part of the hips, a piece of rib and one calf bone 1.55 m long. Blue: never found, the missing back vertebrae and ribs, the second calf bone mirrored from the first, the missing parts of the found bones, shaped to fit its own. Cream: borrowed from relatives, above all Patagotitan.

paras: Each is built at the size of one named find or mount. Argentinosaurus on the Plaza Huincul bones, with a body mainly after Patagotitan. Brachiosaurus on the Chicago skeleton, with neck and head after its relatives. T. rex on SUE, Spinosaurus on the young animal from Morocco. Triceratops on the Smithsonian's mount of about ten animals, whose skull was enlarged when it was rebuilt. Ankylosaurus on the smallest of the three known animals, Stegosaurus on Sophie in London. No colour is known for any of them, so the colours are ours, and neighbours differ where nothing is known. The neck angles of the two long necks are our choice, since no neck bone of either animal exists. That is why their heads stand at almost the same height, though our Argentinosaurus is nine metres longer. Our T. rex shows its mouth open. Shut, its lips most likely covered the teeth.

items.q: Was Spinosaurus bigger than T. rex?
items.a: Longer, and most likely lighter. A grown Spinosaurus was just under 14 m (46 ft) and about 7.4 tonnes in the current model. A big adult T. rex was about 12 m (39 ft) and 8 to 9 tonnes. Ours in the picture is a young Spinosaurus of about 10 m, so there it is the shorter one.

items.q: Was any dinosaur bigger than a blue whale?
items.a: No, by what is known. NOAA, the US ocean agency, calls the blue whale the largest animal ever to live on our planet. Most grown ones are 23 to 27 m long, the largest about 30 m (98 ft). Argentinosaurus at about 30 to 35 m was about as long. Only one land claim was ever put near the weight of the largest whales, the lost Indian find, and its bones are gone.

paras: Museum of Ages is a digital museum, made by a nonprofit. Free entry, no account. In the animal wing these seven will stand among the others. The Leonardo da Vinci wing shows what a finished wing looks like.

A Spinosaurus with a tall sail and a deep tail, the pale outline of a larger adult behind it, beside a grey person who reaches its hip.
items.line: The Spinosaurus from the row, on its own: the sail, the tail, the water, and why an adult was longer than ours.

items.alt: A woolly mammoth from the side in a dark brown coat: high domed head, sloping back, two curved tusks, a mark at the shoulder. The grey person beside him stands lower than the tusk tips.
items.line: Not a dinosaur but an ice age relative of the elephants: a Siberian bull stood about 2.7 to 2.9 m at the shoulder. Ours is one real bull found frozen in 1900, beside a person.

items.alt: A Brachiosaurus from the side, its long neck raised in a gentle curve, the front legs longer than the hind legs, the tail off the ground, beside a grey person who could walk under its belly, a short bar marking the head's top.
items.line: The Brachiosaurus from the row, on its own: about 22 to 25 m long by a reconstruction, a height nobody measured, and why Berlin's famous skeleton is its relative Giraffatitan.

items.alt: A Triceratops from the side: a wide frill behind the head, two long horns over the eyes, a short one on the nose, four legs. Beside it a grey person who reaches about two thirds of the way up its back.
items.line: The Triceratops from the row, on its own: its skull against a person, the Washington skeleton of about ten animals, Torosaurus, and what the bones say about T. rex.

items.alt: An Ankylosaurus from the side: a low, wide body under rows of bony plates, a broad head carried low, four short legs and a straight tail ending in a flat club. Beside it a grey person, as tall as the top of its back over the hips.
items.line: The Ankylosaurus from the row, on its own: its club and armour against a person, what was found of it, and what the bones say about T. rex.

items.alt: A Stegosaurus from the side: a small low head, two rows of tall plates along the arched back, two of its four tail spikes, the front legs shorter than the hind legs. Beside it a grey person whose head stays below the top of its back.
items.line: The Stegosaurus from the row, on its own: its plates and tail spikes against a person, Sophie in London, and the “second brain” story.
